- agent-workflows:do-task: Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
judges whether it finished. - Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for
choosing what to work on, not for opening a change request, and not for deciding whether
the result is good enough — each of those is somebody else's job.

- agent-workflows:file-issue: Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on, and
copies the session log beside it wherever one can be had — always attempted, never a
reason to withhold the issue. Decides first whether the thing needs tracking at all,
searches for an existing issue before creating a second one, quotes the request in the
words it was made in rather than paraphrasing it, and states an acceptance test someone
else can check. Creates the portal every later step resolves back to. - Use whenever work is identified but not started, of any kind — not only code. Code:
"this is broken", "raise a bug", "we should track this", "someone should fix that".
Docs: "the README is wrong", "nobody can find how to run this", "that page is stale",
"this needs writing up". Environment: "staging is on the old version", "we should
upgrade that", "this config drifted", "we need a bigger instance". Operations: "the cert
expires next week", "someone has to rotate that key", "we need to migrate the data",
"that job needs re-running". Also the generic ones: "file an issue", "that's a separate
problem", "let's do that later", "add it to the backlog". Reach for it when a session
surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
goes unrecorded, and when the thing is an act to perform rather than code to write. Not
for a question, a thing already underway, or a fix smaller than the issue describing it.

- agent-workflows:gen-readme: Writes a project's README from the code: researches current README convention on the
web, studies the repo from its ground truth rather than its existing docs, finds the key
points a newcomer needs first, draws every one of them as an SVG rendered to PNG, and
writes the file. Produces the README only — it does not open a PR, and review-readme
gates what it wrote. - Use whenever a README is about to be created or edited — before writing one from
scratch, and before changing an existing one. Covers "write the README", "generate a
README for this project", "our README is stale, redo it", "update the README", "document
this repo for newcomers", "write a README for ../other-repo" — and applies even when the
request is to touch one section rather than the whole file.

- agent-workflows:land-pr: Merges an approved change request and cleans up after it: the code lands in the default
branch, the branch is gone, the issue closes, the labels clear. Asks a person outright
whether the change was reviewed and tested at this exact head, records that answer, and
pins the merge to that SHA so a head that moved cannot slip through. Refuses to merge
without the answer. - Use when an open change request should land — "merge it", "merge PR 30", "land it",
"ship it", "close out #27", "the PR is approved", "merge and clean up". Being told to run
this is a request to reach the human gate, never the answer to it. Not for opening a
change request, and not for work that ends in evidence rather than a diff.

- agent-workflows:open-pr: Pushes a committed branch and opens the change request that carries it to a human, linked
to its issue so the issue closes on merge rather than by hand. Moves the commits onto a
branch first when they landed on the default one, gets the closure keyword right, and
stops for review. It does not merge, and it does not judge whether the work is good;
something before it did that. - Use when reviewed work is ready for a human to look at — "open a PR", "raise the merge
request", "push this up", "ship it", "put it up for review", "my commits are on main, get
them onto a branch". Reach for it after the work has been judged done, and when someone
says ship it meaning make it reviewable. Not for work that ends in evidence rather than a
diff, which closes on its issue and never reaches a change request. Not for merging.

- agent-workflows:plan-work: Splits work too large for one issue into issues that can each be delivered on their own,
and groups them with whatever the project already uses to group things — a milestone, a
project board, an epic. Decides first whether splitting is warranted at all, since most
work is not, and never invents a grouping the platform already provides. - Use when one issue is holding more than one deliverable — "break this down", "what are
the tasks", "this is too big", "split it", "that's really three things", "plan this
out", "make tickets for this". Also when take-issue reports that an issue is more than
one task, which is the case that arrives without anyone asking for a plan. Not for
ordinary work that happens to have several steps, and not for filing a single issue.

- agent-workflows:reporting-outcomes: Reports work in two lines and a question — the verdict, the one next step, and whether
the reader wants it run or wants the detail. Findings, what was checked, risks and
decisions are prepared and held; the reader acts on the next step or asks. Only a
blocked or failed next step brings its blocker up with it. Replaces the reply that mixes
progress, findings, reasoning and status into a narrative the reader has to mine. - Use whenever writing back about work — what was done, what was found, whether it worked,
where things stand, what is left, what broke, what is blocked — and the answer runs
longer than a line. Covers the everyday reply, not only a formal gate: a status update,
a summary of a run, a review verdict, a handoff note, an answer to "how did it go" or
"where are we". Reach for it even when nobody said the word "report", even when the
reply feels short enough to wing, and even when the news is good. The buried verdict is
the failure this prevents, and it is invisible to the person writing it.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-artifacts: Gates the tooling an agent reads — skills, commands, rules, CLAUDE.md — asking whether

talk track and wrong in a test case. Then runs check-prose.sh to locate the mechanical

- agent-workflows:reviewing-typography: Reviews how a human-read document looks — a README, prose and tables in docs/, an HTML

space the groups so the inner gap is smaller than the outer one, emphasize by dimming
what is not the point rather than shouting what is, hold the level count low, and judge
the page whole rather than section by section. Judges the look; the words are a separate
review. - Use whenever a document a person will read is written or restructured — a README, a

1	# The workflow redesign — design, state, and what is left
2	
3	Last updated 2026-08-16. Two units are built and committed; three are unbuilt or unrevised.
4	This file is the design record, not a proposal — where it disagrees with a shipped skill,
5	the skill wins and this file is wrong.
6	
7	## Where it stands
8	
9	| Unit | Status | Fires on | Platform verb | Outstanding |
10	|---|---|---|---|---|
11	| `file-issue` | **done** `409df41` | "this is broken", "we should track this" | `issue create` | Session mechanism is now known and §3 describes the wrong one. Templates cover bug + task only — needs the kind fork |
12	| `take-issue` | **done** `3a7f90a` | "work on #42", "what's next" | `issue edit --add-assignee` + branch | Branch is unconditional; must depend on whether a diff is coming |
13	| `do-task` | **not done** | "implement it", "run the migration" | commits, **or** the act itself | Everything. **The chain dead-ends here** |
14	| `reviewing-finish` | **needs rewrite** | after `do-task`, every time | comments on the issue | Exists from the old chain doing a different job. Becomes the **router** — see below |
15	| `open-pr` | **needs revision** | "open a PR", "ship it" | `pr create` / `mr create` | Exists as `ship-create-pr`: 7 `project-profile` refs, old report shape, old name |
16	| `land-pr` | **needs revision** | "merge it" | `pr merge` / `mr merge` | Exists as `ship-merge`: same three, plus the outcome contract |
17	| `save-session` | **not a unit** | — | writes `.sessions/` | Internal to `file-issue`, like a private method |
18	
19	Two done, one to build, one to rewrite, two to revise, one absorbed.
20	
21	## The design
22	
23	**This is GitHub Flow, unit by unit — not a workflow on top of it.** Its canonical
24	lifecycle is branch off main, open a change request, review, merge, delete the branch.
25	GitLab Flow is that plus environment branches where a project needs them. The units map
26	onto it one to one, branch deletion included, and spare the user remembering which CLI says
27	`pr` and which says `mr`.
28	
29	```
30	  ┌─ PLANNING PLANE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
31	  │  epic · milestone · iteration · Project board                         │
32	  │  Lives on the platform. Not built here — a skill would hand-roll it.  │
33	  └────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
34	                                   │ groups the issues below
35	                                   ▼
36	                    something said in a session
37	                              │
38	                              ▼
39	                    ┌─────────────────────┐  needs tracking?
40	                  ✓ │     file-issue      │ ──── no ────► answered here.
41	                    │  decides the KIND   │               A verdict, not a skip.
42	                    └──────────┬──────────┘
43	                               │ yes
44	        ┌────────────┬─────────┼─────────┬────────────┐
45	        ▼            ▼         ▼         ▼            ▼
46	      code       document   environment  operation   (…)
47	     bug/feat    README      provision   run/rotate
48	                 spec        upgrade     migrate
49	        └────────────┴─────────┼─────────┴────────────┘
50	                               ▼
51	     .sessions/<uuid>.jsonl   ╔═════════════════╗
52	     raw, verbatim,       ──► ║    ISSUE #42    ║
53	     always tried,            ║    the portal   ║
54	     never a blocker          ╚════════╤════════╝
55	                                       ▼
56	                             ┌───────────────────┐
57	                           ✓ │    take-issue     │ ◄──────────┐
58	                             └─────────┬─────────┘            │
59	                                 pickable? ── no ──► refuse + │
60	                                       │ yes        offer fix ┘
61	                                       ▼
62	                              claim: assignee + label
63	                              + branch ONLY if a diff is coming
64	                                       ▼
65	                             ┌───────────────────┐ ◄────────────────┐
66	                           · │      do-task      │                  │
67	                             └─────────┬─────────┘                  │
68	                        writes files ──┤── or performs the act      │
69	                                       ▼                            │
70	                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐         │
71	                  ! │         reviewing-finish            │         │
72	                    │   what state is this ACTUALLY in?   │         │
73	                    └──┬────┬────────┬─────────┬──────────┘         │
74	                       │    │        │         │                    │
75	              not      │    │ half   │ stuck   │ more than          │
76	             started / │    │ done,  │         │ one task           │
77	             blocked   │    │ fixable│         │                    │
78	                       ▼    └────────┼─────────┼──── back to do-task┘
79	              back to the issue      ▼         ▼
80	              comment · unassign   back to   route to the
81	              · say why            the issue PLANNING PLANE
82	                                   escalate  (decompose)
83	                       │
84	                     done
85	                       ▼
86	        ┌──── does it end in a DIFF? ────┐
87	    yes │                                │ no
88	        ▼                                ▼
89	┌───────────────────┐          record the evidence on
90	│      open-pr      │ ~        the issue — command run,
91	└─────────┬─────────┘          output, before/after state
92	          │ ◄── [human reviews + tests]  │
93	          ▼                              ▼
94	┌───────────────────┐            close the issue
95	│      land-pr      │ ~          by hand, with that
96	└─────────┬─────────┘            evidence attached
97	  merged · closed · branch gone  │
98	          └───────────┬──────────┘
99	                      ▼
100	                    done
101	
102	  ✓ built   · to build   ! to rewrite   ~ exists, needs revision
103	  review is a gate inside open-pr → land-pr, not a unit
104	```
105	
106	### The router
107	
108	`reviewing-finish` answers the question the flow used to assume away: **`do-task` finished,
109	but finished at what?** Five states, five destinations:
110	
111	| State | Goes to |
112	|---|---|
113	| **done** | the diff-or-evidence fork |
114	| **half done, and the rest is solvable** | back to `do-task` |
115	| **stuck** | back to the issue — comment with what blocked it, unassign, say why |
116	| **more than one task in here** | the planning plane, to decompose |
117	| **not started, or blocked** | back to the issue |
118	
119	Only one of the five reaches a change request. That is the point: a unit that always
120	advanced would be a formality, and the four other states are the ones that go unrecorded
121	today — work quietly half-finished, or stuck with nobody told.
122	
123	### The portal
124	
125	The issue is the one addressable thing everything resolves back to. When the user says
126	"merge it" they say nothing about the issue, the branch, or the session — the unit walks
127	back: PR → issue → branch → log. Without that join, every unit would need the user to carry
128	context forward, which is the drift this design exists to remove.
129	
130	State lives on the platform. The toolkit holds none of its own: no story file, no plan file,
131	no index. The log is a record; the portal is the state.
132	
133	### Two forks decide the path
134	
135	**Kind**, at `file-issue`: code · document · environment · operation. Four readers, four
136	acceptance tests. A template set offering only bug and task assumes every issue is a software
137	change — which is what the shipped skill currently assumes, and is the first thing to widen.
138	
139	**Diff or evidence**, after `do-task`. Work ending in a patch goes to `open-pr` and closes by
140	merging. Work ending in an observation — a cert rotated, a cluster restarted, data migrated —
141	closes by hand with the command, its output, and the before-and-after state on the issue.
142	The branch follows the same fork: no diff, no branch.
143	
144	### Triggering, in the user's words
145	
146	| The user says | Portal? | What happens |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| "how does X work", "what do you think" | none needed | answered in session; nothing created |
149	| "this is broken", "we should track this" | none yet | `file-issue` creates the portal |
150	| "just fix this typo" | none needed | done in session; a portal costs more than the work |
151	| "what's next", "work on #42" | exists | `take-issue` reads portal and log, then claims |
152	| "implement it", "run the migration" | exists | `do-task` — one writes files, one does not |
153	| "open a PR" | exists | `open-pr` — closure keyword back to the portal |
154	| "merge it" | exists | `land-pr` — resolves PR → portal, then cleans up |
155	
156	**Row 2 versus row 3 is the judgment the workflow lives or dies on.** Too eager and every
157	remark becomes an issue nobody closes; too reluctant and work happens with no record.
158	
159	## The session log
160	
161	An **accuracy aid, not a requirement** — always attempted, never a reason to withhold an
162	issue. Raw, whole, unedited: the moment anyone decides what mattered, the thing that
163	mattered and was not obvious is gone.
164	
165	**The mechanism, now known.** Claude Code writes a transcript per session to
166	`~/.claude/projects/<project-slug>/<session-uuid>.jsonl`, alongside subagent transcripts and
167	tool-result files in a directory of the same name. The record is that file copied verbatim
168	into `.sessions/` — not a rendering of it. A markdown view is a filter, however careful, and
169	can always be regenerated from the source since nothing was dropped.
170	
171	**Read as background knowledge, never as specification.**
172	
173	| Source | Authority |
174	|---|---|
175	| the code | binds on **reality** — what is true now |
176	| the issue | binds on **scope** — what this change may touch |
177	| the log | **informs only** — never binds |
178	
179	A log that seems to forbid something is not a constraint; it is a previous person's
180	situation. This is the rule that stops a record becoming the frozen spec it replaced.
181	
182	**Memory, not history.** Humans keep memory and consult it when relevant; they keep
183	principles and break them when conditions change. The log is history in storage and memory
184	in use — rawness stops anything being pre-judged when written, and *informs-never-binds*
185	stops it ossifying when read.
186	
187	**Validated independently.** The open Zed discussion on per-repo agent history proposes
188	storing threads under a project directory, and its author moved from markdown to a JSON
189	*agent trace* format specifically because markdown export is lossy — it drops the context
190	selected, the file state at the moment of inclusion, the model, and the reasoning steps.
191	Same drift, named by someone else. The standard is unsettled, so: raw JSONL now.
192	
193	**Two honest costs.** Transcripts are large — 12 MB for this project's five sessions — and
194	an agent reading one spends context before starting. And nobody can reopen an exported
195	conversation at full fidelity: a log is a record, not resumable state.
196	
197	## Build order
198	
199	1. **`do-task`** — the chain dead-ends without it; everything else is an enhancement
200	2. **`reviewing-finish`** — rewrite as the router. Without it `do-task` always advances,
201	   and four of the five real states go unrecorded
202	3. **`open-pr`** — revision, and it retires the two naming conventions living side by side
203	4. **`land-pr`** — revision; keep its human gate unchanged, let it absorb the review step
204	5. *spine complete — runnable end to end on one real issue*
205	6. **`file-issue` §3** — point it at the real mechanism; it currently describes a markdown
206	   rendering that no longer exists
207	7. **`plan-work`** — only if the spine shows decomposition is real here, and only mapped onto
208	   the platform's own planning objects
209	
210	## Open questions
211	
212	| # | Question | Lean |
213	|---|---|---|
214	| A | ~~How a session transcript is obtained~~ | **Answered.** `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<uuid>.jsonl`. Committed at `1dfcc36`, 22 files, 12 MB, byte-identical to source |
215	| B | Whether a 12 MB log per project stays workable as sessions accumulate | Unknown, and only running it will tell. Pruning is ruled out; an index or a per-issue line range is the lever if it bites |
216	
217	Everything else that was open has been decided — below.
218	
219	## Settled, with reasons
220	
221	Kept so nobody re-proposes what was already rejected.
222	
223	### The merge contract
224	
225	**Merge means one thing: the code is in the default branch, and the branch is merged and
226	deleted.** Nothing else about it is interesting to the person asking.
227	
228	How that outcome is reached is the repository's business — required approvals, protected
229	branch rules, CI that must go green, a merge train, environment promotion, whatever the
230	project's own process demands. `land-pr` does whatever that repo requires to reach the
231	outcome, and does not ask the user to know which.
232	
233	**If it cannot reach the outcome, that is a verdict**, not a partial reported as success:
234	a failure with what blocked it, or a revise with what must change first. The one thing it
235	must never do is report *merged* when the code is not in the default branch.
236	
237	This retires the environment-branch question. The distinction between GitHub Flow and
238	GitLab Flow's promotion chain is a route, and routes are the repo's to define. A unit that
239	froze one would be the invented mechanism this design exists to avoid.
240	
241	### Closing an issue that ends in evidence
242	
243	Two halves, and only one is a step:
244	
245	- **Performing** the close, for work the agent just did — inside `do-task`. The act and the
246	  record of it are one thing: you ran the command, you have the output.
247	- **Noticing** that some *other* issue is already stale or satisfied — a shared obligation
248	  in every unit that touches an issue, not a unit of its own. The trigger is discovery
249	  while doing something else, and discovery is not a phrasing anybody types.
250	
251	**The noticing half offers; it never closes.** An issue that looks done can be a false
252	positive, and closing one wrongly is worse than leaving it open — it leaves the board while
253	the work stands undone. So it is a line in the report attached to whatever the agent was
254	actually doing: *"#38 looks already satisfied by <evidence>; close it?"*
255	
256	That is cleanup without a sweep. A board tidied continuously by work already happening,
257	rather than a paperwork task nobody reaches for.
258	
259	### The rest
260	
261	| Decision | Outcome |
262	|---|---|
263	| Story files | Dropped. `docs/stories/` deleted; nothing writes or reads one |
264	| Where logs live | `.sessions/`, outside `docs/` so no doc reviewer treats them as prose |
265	| Log format | The raw `.jsonl` Claude Code writes, copied verbatim. A markdown rendering is a filter, and regenerable from the source anyway |
266	| Who writes the log | `file-issue`, wherever one can be had |
267	| Pruning | Never. Pruning is summarising with a longer interval |

# The workflow redesign — design, state, and what is left

Last updated 2026-08-16. Two units are built and committed; three are unbuilt or unrevised.
This file is the design record, not a proposal — where it disagrees with a shipped skill,
the skill wins and this file is wrong.

## Where it stands

| Unit | Status | Fires on | Platform verb | Outstanding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `file-issue` | **done** `409df41` | "this is broken", "we should track this" | `issue create` | Session mechanism is now known and §3 describes the wrong one. Templates cover bug + task only — needs the kind fork |
| `take-issue` | **done** `3a7f90a` | "work on #42", "what's next" | `issue edit --add-assignee` + branch | Branch is unconditional; must depend on whether a diff is coming |
| `do-task` | **not done** | "implement it", "run the migration" | commits, **or** the act itself | Everything. **The chain dead-ends here** |
| `reviewing-finish` | **needs rewrite** | after `do-task`, every time | comments on the issue | Exists from the old chain doing a different job. Becomes the **router** — see below |
| `open-pr` | **needs revision** | "open a PR", "ship it" | `pr create` / `mr create` | Exists as `ship-create-pr`: 7 `project-profile` refs, old report shape, old name |
| `land-pr` | **needs revision** | "merge it" | `pr merge` / `mr merge` | Exists as `ship-merge`: same three, plus the outcome contract |
| `save-session` | **not a unit** | — | writes `.sessions/` | Internal to `file-issue`, like a private method |

Two done, one to build, one to rewrite, two to revise, one absorbed.

## The design

**This is GitHub Flow, unit by unit — not a workflow on top of it.** Its canonical
lifecycle is branch off main, open a change request, review, merge, delete the branch.
GitLab Flow is that plus environment branches where a project needs them. The units map
onto it one to one, branch deletion included, and spare the user remembering which CLI says
`pr` and which says `mr`.

```
  ┌─ PLANNING PLANE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  epic · milestone · iteration · Project board                         │
  │  Lives on the platform. Not built here — a skill would hand-roll it.  │
  └────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ groups the issues below
                                   ▼
                    something said in a session
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐  needs tracking?
                  ✓ │     file-issue      │ ──── no ────► answered here.
                    │  decides the KIND   │               A verdict, not a skip.
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │ yes
        ┌────────────┬─────────┼─────────┬────────────┐
        ▼            ▼         ▼         ▼            ▼
      code       document   environment  operation   (…)
     bug/feat    README      provision   run/rotate
                 spec        upgrade     migrate
        └────────────┴─────────┼─────────┴────────────┘
                               ▼
     .sessions/<uuid>.jsonl   ╔═════════════════╗
     raw, verbatim,       ──► ║    ISSUE #42    ║
     always tried,            ║    the portal   ║
     never a blocker          ╚════════╤════════╝
                                       ▼
                             ┌───────────────────┐
                           ✓ │    take-issue     │ ◄──────────┐
                             └─────────┬─────────┘            │
                                 pickable? ── no ──► refuse + │
                                       │ yes        offer fix ┘
                                       ▼
                              claim: assignee + label
                              + branch ONLY if a diff is coming
                                       ▼
                             ┌───────────────────┐ ◄────────────────┐
                           · │      do-task      │                  │
                             └─────────┬─────────┘                  │
                        writes files ──┤── or performs the act      │
                                       ▼                            │
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐         │
                  ! │         reviewing-finish            │         │
                    │   what state is this ACTUALLY in?   │         │
                    └──┬────┬────────┬─────────┬──────────┘         │
                       │    │        │         │                    │
              not      │    │ half   │ stuck   │ more than          │
             started / │    │ done,  │         │ one task           │
             blocked   │    │ fixable│         │                    │
                       ▼    └────────┼─────────┼──── back to do-task┘
              back to the issue      ▼         ▼
              comment · unassign   back to   route to the
              · say why            the issue PLANNING PLANE
                                   escalate  (decompose)
                       │
                     done
                       ▼
        ┌──── does it end in a DIFF? ────┐
    yes │                                │ no
        ▼                                ▼
┌───────────────────┐          record the evidence on
│      open-pr      │ ~        the issue — command run,
└─────────┬─────────┘          output, before/after state
          │ ◄── [human reviews + tests]  │
          ▼                              ▼
┌───────────────────┐            close the issue
│      land-pr      │ ~          by hand, with that
└─────────┬─────────┘            evidence attached
  merged · closed · branch gone  │
          └───────────┬──────────┘
                      ▼
                    done

  ✓ built   · to build   ! to rewrite   ~ exists, needs revision
  review is a gate inside open-pr → land-pr, not a unit
```

### The router

`reviewing-finish` answers the question the flow used to assume away: **`do-task` finished,
but finished at what?** Five states, five destinations:

| State | Goes to |
|---|---|
| **done** | the diff-or-evidence fork |
| **half done, and the rest is solvable** | back to `do-task` |
| **stuck** | back to the issue — comment with what blocked it, unassign, say why |
| **more than one task in here** | the planning plane, to decompose |
| **not started, or blocked** | back to the issue |

Only one of the five reaches a change request. That is the point: a unit that always
advanced would be a formality, and the four other states are the ones that go unrecorded
today — work quietly half-finished, or stuck with nobody told.

### The portal

The issue is the one addressable thing everything resolves back to. When the user says
"merge it" they say nothing about the issue, the branch, or the session — the unit walks
back: PR → issue → branch → log. Without that join, every unit would need the user to carry
context forward, which is the drift this design exists to remove.

State lives on the platform. The toolkit holds none of its own: no story file, no plan file,
no index. The log is a record; the portal is the state.

### Two forks decide the path

**Kind**, at `file-issue`: code · document · environment · operation. Four readers, four
acceptance tests. A template set offering only bug and task assumes every issue is a software
change — which is what the shipped skill currently assumes, and is the first thing to widen.

**Diff or evidence**, after `do-task`. Work ending in a patch goes to `open-pr` and closes by
merging. Work ending in an observation — a cert rotated, a cluster restarted, data migrated —
closes by hand with the command, its output, and the before-and-after state on the issue.
The branch follows the same fork: no diff, no branch.

### Triggering, in the user's words

| The user says | Portal? | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| "how does X work", "what do you think" | none needed | answered in session; nothing created |
| "this is broken", "we should track this" | none yet | `file-issue` creates the portal |
| "just fix this typo" | none needed | done in session; a portal costs more than the work |
| "what's next", "work on #42" | exists | `take-issue` reads portal and log, then claims |
| "implement it", "run the migration" | exists | `do-task` — one writes files, one does not |
| "open a PR" | exists | `open-pr` — closure keyword back to the portal |
| "merge it" | exists | `land-pr` — resolves PR → portal, then cleans up |

**Row 2 versus row 3 is the judgment the workflow lives or dies on.** Too eager and every
remark becomes an issue nobody closes; too reluctant and work happens with no record.

## The session log

An **accuracy aid, not a requirement** — always attempted, never a reason to withhold an
issue. Raw, whole, unedited: the moment anyone decides what mattered, the thing that
mattered and was not obvious is gone.

**The mechanism, now known.** Claude Code writes a transcript per session to
`~/.claude/projects/<project-slug>/<session-uuid>.jsonl`, alongside subagent transcripts and
tool-result files in a directory of the same name. The record is that file copied verbatim
into `.sessions/` — not a rendering of it. A markdown view is a filter, however careful, and
can always be regenerated from the source since nothing was dropped.

**Read as background knowledge, never as specification.**

| Source | Authority |
|---|---|
| the code | binds on **reality** — what is true now |
| the issue | binds on **scope** — what this change may touch |
| the log | **informs only** — never binds |

A log that seems to forbid something is not a constraint; it is a previous person's
situation. This is the rule that stops a record becoming the frozen spec it replaced.

**Memory, not history.** Humans keep memory and consult it when relevant; they keep
principles and break them when conditions change. The log is history in storage and memory
in use — rawness stops anything being pre-judged when written, and *informs-never-binds*
stops it ossifying when read.

**Validated independently.** The open Zed discussion on per-repo agent history proposes
storing threads under a project directory, and its author moved from markdown to a JSON
*agent trace* format specifically because markdown export is lossy — it drops the context
selected, the file state at the moment of inclusion, the model, and the reasoning steps.
Same drift, named by someone else. The standard is unsettled, so: raw JSONL now.

**Two honest costs.** Transcripts are large — 12 MB for this project's five sessions — and
an agent reading one spends context before starting. And nobody can reopen an exported
conversation at full fidelity: a log is a record, not resumable state.

## Build order

1. **`do-task`** — the chain dead-ends without it; everything else is an enhancement
2. **`reviewing-finish`** — rewrite as the router. Without it `do-task` always advances,
   and four of the five real states go unrecorded
3. **`open-pr`** — revision, and it retires the two naming conventions living side by side
4. **`land-pr`** — revision; keep its human gate unchanged, let it absorb the review step
5. *spine complete — runnable end to end on one real issue*
6. **`file-issue` §3** — point it at the real mechanism; it currently describes a markdown
   rendering that no longer exists
7. **`plan-work`** — only if the spine shows decomposition is real here, and only mapped onto
   the platform's own planning objects

## Open questions

| # | Question | Lean |
|---|---|---|
| A | ~~How a session transcript is obtained~~ | **Answered.** `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<uuid>.jsonl`. Committed at `1dfcc36`, 22 files, 12 MB, byte-identical to source |
| B | Whether a 12 MB log per project stays workable as sessions accumulate | Unknown, and only running it will tell. Pruning is ruled out; an index or a per-issue line range is the lever if it bites |

Everything else that was open has been decided — below.

## Settled, with reasons

Kept so nobody re-proposes what was already rejected.

### The merge contract

**Merge means one thing: the code is in the default branch, and the branch is merged and
deleted.** Nothing else about it is interesting to the person asking.

How that outcome is reached is the repository's business — required approvals, protected
branch rules, CI that must go green, a merge train, environment promotion, whatever the
project's own process demands. `land-pr` does whatever that repo requires to reach the
outcome, and does not ask the user to know which.

**If it cannot reach the outcome, that is a verdict**, not a partial reported as success:
a failure with what blocked it, or a revise with what must change first. The one thing it
must never do is report *merged* when the code is not in the default branch.

This retires the environment-branch question. The distinction between GitHub Flow and
GitLab Flow's promotion chain is a route, and routes are the repo's to define. A unit that
froze one would be the invented mechanism this design exists to avoid.

### Closing an issue that ends in evidence

Two halves, and only one is a step:

- **Performing** the close, for work the agent just did — inside `do-task`. The act and the
  record of it are one thing: you ran the command, you have the output.
- **Noticing** that some *other* issue is already stale or satisfied — a shared obligation
  in every unit that touches an issue, not a unit of its own. The trigger is discovery
  while doing something else, and discovery is not a phrasing anybody types.

**The noticing half offers; it never closes.** An issue that looks done can be a false
positive, and closing one wrongly is worse than leaving it open — it leaves the board while
the work stands undone. So it is a line in the report attached to whatever the agent was
actually doing: *"#38 looks already satisfied by <evidence>; close it?"*

That is cleanup without a sweep. A board tidied continuously by work already happening,
rather than a paperwork task nobody reaches for.

### The rest

| Decision | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Story files | Dropped. `docs/stories/` deleted; nothing writes or reads one |
| Where logs live | `.sessions/`, outside `docs/` so no doc reviewer treats them as prose |
| Log format | The raw `.jsonl` Claude Code writes, copied verbatim. A markdown rendering is a filter, and regenerable from the source anyway |
| Who writes the log | `file-issue`, wherever one can be had |
| Pruning | Never. Pruning is summarising with a longer interval |
| `save-session` as a unit | **No.** Internal to `file-issue`, like a private method. It gets exported only when a second unit needs it, and that is a decision for then |
| Templates per kind | **Yes, and more of them.** A source file carries its own contract; a markdown file carries none, so the template *is* the contract. This is the thing agents handle worst without structure |
| `review-work` | **CUT.** Neither flow has review as an artifact — it is the step between opening and merging, and it changes no state `open-pr` and `land-pr` do not own. A gate inside that pair |
| `plan-work` | **Deferred and rescoped.** It was a hand-rolled epic. Both platforms ship a planning layer and they ship different ones — epics are group-level and paid on GitLab, GitHub uses Projects with sub-issues. A unit inventing decomposition drifts from the team's actual board |
| Eight units | **Six.** The two above came off once the platform's own flow was checked |

**Sources:** [Zed discussion #45334 — per-repo agent history](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/discussions/45334) · [GitLab Flow best practices](https://about.gitlab.com/topics/version-control/what-are-gitlab-flow-best-practices/) · [Branching strategies compared](https://www.deployhq.com/blog/5-effective-git-branching-strategies-for-streamlined-development) · [GitLab epics vs milestones vs iterations](https://forum.gitlab.com/t/epics-vs-milestones-vs-iterations/77973)

2	name: reporting-outcomes
3	description: |
4	  Reports work in two lines and a question — the verdict, the one next step, and whether
5	  the reader wants it run or wants the detail. Findings, what was checked, risks and
6	  decisions are prepared and held; the reader acts on the next step or asks. Only a
7	  blocked or failed next step brings its blocker up with it. Replaces the reply that mixes
8	  progress, findings, reasoning and status into a narrative the reader has to mine.
9	when_to_use: |
10	  Use whenever writing back about work — what was done, what was found, whether it worked,
11	  where things stand, what is left, what broke, what is blocked — and the answer runs
12	  longer than a line. Covers the everyday reply, not only a formal gate: a status update,
13	  a summary of a run, a review verdict, a handoff note, an answer to "how did it go" or
14	  "where are we". Reach for it even when nobody said the word "report", even when the
15	  reply feels short enough to wing, and even when the news is good. The buried verdict is
16	  the failure this prevents, and it is invisible to the person writing it.
17	---
18	
19	# Reporting outcomes
20	
21	**Under 30 seconds, or it failed.** The reader wants two things — *is it good, and what
22	happens now*. Everything else is yours to hold until they ask.
23	
24	Volume is not the cost. **Interpretation burden** is: information arriving faster than
25	meaning can be extracted from it. A reader handed everything and told nothing does your
26	judging at their rate.
27	
28	## The default: two lines and a question
29	
30	    <VERDICT> — <the one thing that decides it>.
31	    Next: <one step>.
32	    <run it, or see the detail?>
33	
34	Stop there.
35	
36	    PASS — all five findings closed.
37	    Next: nothing. Ready for use.
38	    Want the detail?
39	
40	    REVISE — 7 findings, 2 of them break checks that were reported working.
41	    Next: fix all 7 in one pass.
42	    Run it, or see the findings?
43	
44	    IN FLIGHT — 6 of 9 scenarios clear, 3 failing on one cause.
45	    Next: fix the shared cause and re-run, ~20 min.
46	    Want the failing three?
47	
48	That is the whole report. Not a summary of one.
49	
50	### The offer is the last line
51	
52	**If the message contains an offer, nothing follows it.** Not a paragraph of context, not
53	the findings the offer was for, not one more useful thing. The question mark ends the
54	message.
55	
56	This is stated as a rule about the *shape of the message* rather than about withholding,
57	because that is the version anyone can check. Look at the text: is there anything after the
58	offer? Withholding is invisible — a message where you held something back and one where you
59	forgot to are identical up to the question and only diverge after it, so "did I withhold"
60	cannot be answered by reading what you wrote.
61	
62	**Asking and then answering is worse than not asking.** It presents a choice and takes it
63	away in the same breath, and it costs the reader the exact attention the two-line shape was
64	built to save. A report that just dumps everything is at least honest about what it is.
65	
66	    ✗  DONE — the parser is fixed.                ✓  DONE — the parser is fixed.
67	       Next: open the change request.                Next: open the change request.
68	       Want the detail?                              Want the detail?
69	                                                  ─── end of message ───
70	       The fix was in the lookahead, which
71	       had been…  ← the offer is now a
72	                    decoration
73	
74	## What is withheld
75	
76	Findings · Checked · Risks · Decisions · Not done · Unresolved · Trace.
77	
78	All of it real, and all of it done — a reader who trusts the verdict never spends a second
79	on it, which is the point rather than a reason to skip the work behind it.
80	
81	## The one exception
82	
83	**A next step that is blocked or failed brings its blocker with it**, because the reader
84	cannot act without it:
85	
86	    BLOCKED — staging credentials missing.
87	    Next: you send them, or I stub the integration and we lose real-path coverage.
88	
89	    FAILED — migration rolled back at step 4 of 7.
90	    Next: I need a call on retry-with-fix or revert to the old schema.
91	
92	**These take no question line.** The choice is already inside Next, and asking again
93	after it is the offered extra this format exists to kill.
94	
95	Nothing else surfaces uninvited. A risk that does not block the next step waits until
96	asked.
97	
98	## When the verdict covers more than one thing
99	
100	**One subject, however many findings inside it, is one verdict and never a table.** An
101	issue fixed across five files with three findings on the way is one thing:
102	
103	    PASS — #42 fixed, tests green.
104	    Next: open the PR.
105	
106	Aggregate only when you judged N independent subjects that each deserve their own verdict —
107	ten skills, a folder of docs. The test: **could the reader act on one without the others?**
108	Ten skills, yes; one issue's five files, no.
109	
110	When they are independent and there are only a few — up to about three — give **one
111	verdict line each and one Next**. Verdicts are cheap to scan; a count the reader has to
112	expand is not:
113	
114	    PASS — reporting-outcomes: aggregation rule added.
115	    PASS — reviewing-artifacts: CUT-sorts-first added.
116	    Next: commit both.
117	
118	Past a handful the list of verdicts becomes its own wall, so line one reports the set:
119	
120	    REVISE — 3 of 10 need work; 1 is a CUT candidate.
121	    Next: fix the 3, starting with the CUT — deleting a file voids its other findings.
122	    See the per-item table?
123	
124	The worst verdict sets the grade, and the line names **every** count — `REVISE` alone
125	hides the CUT, `3 of 10` alone hides what kind of trouble. When the table is asked for it
126	lists **every** item, clean ones included:
127	
128	    | Item | Verdict | Findings |
129	
130	A table of only the failures cannot be told from one that ran out of budget partway. And it
131	is still exactly one next step — ranking N items is the writer's job, not the reader's.
132	
133	## Verdicts and states
134	
135	**A verdict judges; a state describes.** Most work is graded, and some is better described —
136	*half done* and *more than one task* are real outcomes no grade carries. Either way the
137	first word must come from a **declared, fixed set**, never improvised per report, because
138	that is what lets it grade before the sentence is parsed.
139	
140	Judging:
141	
142	`PASS` · `REVISE` · `BLOCKED` · `FAILED` · `IN FLIGHT`
143	
144	Describing: whatever set the unit declares, defined where it declares them.
145	
146	Unfinished work still gets a first word; it changes what the line answers, not whether
147	there is one. **Progress is not a verdict** — "working through the scenarios" is a status,
148	"six of nine clear, three failing on one cause" is a report.
149	
150	## When they ask
151	
152	**Answer the question they asked, and only that one.** Each question has one home:
153	
154	| They ask | Give | Not |
155	|---|---|---|
156	| "what's wrong" / "the findings" | the findings | plus checked, plus trace |
157	| "why" / "why that way" | the reasoning, attached to what it justifies | a standalone rationale section |
158	| "what did you check" / "how do you know" | the commands run and what they printed | a restated verdict |
159	| "is it risky" / "what could bite" | the risks, each with what would resolve it | risks without an ask |
160	| "where" / "which files" | the trace | a narrative of getting there |
161	| "show me everything" | all of it, in the order above | — |
162	
163	**The 30-second cap applies to the detail too.** It is not the place the held-back report
164	finally lands — a second wall of text costs more than the first, because the reader paid a
165	question to get it. If the honest answer does not fit, say what it is and offer the rest:
166	*"12 findings, the 3 that block are below — the other 9 are cosmetic, want them?"*
167	
168	Severity order, tightest useful shape. A table where the rows are peers:
169	
170	    | # | Sev | Location | What's wrong | Smallest fix |
171	
172	**On a PASS, `Checked` is the whole substance** — no findings justify the verdict, so what
173	was actually run is all that makes it worth anything. Name the command and its result.
174	Asserting "verified" without the observation is the costliest slop there is; every later
175	decision rests on it.
176	
177	**Then stop.** Do not re-offer the remaining sections, do not summarise what was just
178	given, and do not close with a next step that was already stated. The answer ends when the
179	question is answered.
180	
181	## Diagrams
182	
183	ASCII only, only in the detail, only when the thing has a **shape** — a sequence, a break
184	in one, a dependency, a before-and-after:
185	
186	    scrape ──► parse ──► ✗ validate ──► load ──► notify
187	                          schema drift          (never ran)
188	
189	One per answer at most. Never in the two-line default. Never for two items, a list that is
190	already a list, or decoration.
191	
192	## When this does not fire
193	
194	A skill that fires on everything turns every reply into a form.
195	
196	- the answer is one fact and the fact is what was asked
197	- an acknowledgement — "pushed", "done", "it's at X"
198	- a discussion, a design proposal, or thinking aloud — a report states a conclusion, it
199	  does not develop one
200	- nothing was judged; a status carrying no judgment is a status, and that is fine
201	
202	## The markers
203	
204	**The buried verdict.** The judgment lands after the narration, so the reader spends the
205	attention the report existed to save — twice, if it is bad news.
206	
207	**The volunteered extra.** Findings, caveats and trace shown unasked, or a "want me to
208	also…" bolted onto the answer. Both spend the reader on something they did not raise, and
209	both tax the two lines that mattered.
210	
211	**Progress dressed as a verdict.** A status with a grade-shaped sentence around it.
212	
213	**Silent omission.** Asked for findings and given four of seven, with nothing saying so.
214	
215	**Confidence not matched to method.** A thing fixed on reading and a thing reproduced then
216	fixed, stated in the same voice. Only the writer knows; say which.

  longer than a line. Covers the everyday reply, not only a formal gate: a status update,
  a summary of a run, a review verdict, a handoff note, an answer to "how did it go" or
  "where are we". Reach for it even when nobody said the word "report", even when the
  reply feels short enough to wing, and even when the news is good. The buried verdict is
  the failure this prevents, and it is invisible to the person writing it.
---

# Reporting outcomes

**Under 30 seconds, or it failed.** The reader wants two things — *is it good, and what
happens now*. Everything else is yours to hold until they ask.

Volume is not the cost. **Interpretation burden** is: information arriving faster than
meaning can be extracted from it. A reader handed everything and told nothing does your
judging at their rate.

## The default: two lines and a question

    <VERDICT> — <the one thing that decides it>.
    Next: <one step>.
    <run it, or see the detail?>

Stop there.

    PASS — all five findings closed.
    Next: nothing. Ready for use.
    Want the detail?

    REVISE — 7 findings, 2 of them break checks that were reported working.
    Next: fix all 7 in one pass.
    Run it, or see the findings?

    IN FLIGHT — 6 of 9 scenarios clear, 3 failing on one cause.
    Next: fix the shared cause and re-run, ~20 min.
    Want the failing three?

That is the whole report. Not a summary of one.

### The offer is the last line

**If the message contains an offer, nothing follows it.** Not a paragraph of context, not
the findings the offer was for, not one more useful thing. The question mark ends the
message.

This is stated as a rule about the *shape of the message* rather than about withholding,
because that is the version anyone can check. Look at the text: is there anything after the
offer? Withholding is invisible — a message where you held something back and one where you
forgot to are identical up to the question and only diverge after it, so "did I withhold"
cannot be answered by reading what you wrote.

**Asking and then answering is worse than not asking.** It presents a choice and takes it
away in the same breath, and it costs the reader the exact attention the two-line shape was
built to save. A report that just dumps everything is at least honest about what it is.

    ✗  DONE — the parser is fixed.                ✓  DONE — the parser is fixed.
       Next: open the change request.                Next: open the change request.
       Want the detail?                              Want the detail?
                                                  ─── end of message ───
       The fix was in the lookahead, which
       had been…  ← the offer is now a
                    decoration

## What is withheld

Findings · Checked · Risks · Decisions · Not done · Unresolved · Trace.

All of it real, and all of it done — a reader who trusts the verdict never spends a second
on it, which is the point rather than a reason to skip the work behind it.

## The one exception

**A next step that is blocked or failed brings its blocker with it**, because the reader
cannot act without it:

    BLOCKED — staging credentials missing.
    Next: you send them, or I stub the integration and we lose real-path coverage.

    FAILED — migration rolled back at step 4 of 7.
    Next: I need a call on retry-with-fix or revert to the old schema.

**These take no question line.** The choice is already inside Next, and asking again
after it is the offered extra this format exists to kill.

Nothing else surfaces uninvited. A risk that does not block the next step waits until
asked.

## When the verdict covers more than one thing

**One subject, however many findings inside it, is one verdict and never a table.** An
issue fixed across five files with three findings on the way is one thing:

    PASS — #42 fixed, tests green.
    Next: open the PR.

Aggregate only when you judged N independent subjects that each deserve their own verdict —
ten skills, a folder of docs. The test: **could the reader act on one without the others?**
Ten skills, yes; one issue's five files, no.

When they are independent and there are only a few — up to about three — give **one
verdict line each and one Next**. Verdicts are cheap to scan; a count the reader has to
expand is not:

    PASS — reporting-outcomes: aggregation rule added.
    PASS — reviewing-artifacts: CUT-sorts-first added.
    Next: commit both.

Past a handful the list of verdicts becomes its own wall, so line one reports the set:

    REVISE — 3 of 10 need work; 1 is a CUT candidate.
    Next: fix the 3, starting with the CUT — deleting a file voids its other findings.
    See the per-item table?

The worst verdict sets the grade, and the line names **every** count — `REVISE` alone
hides the CUT, `3 of 10` alone hides what kind of trouble. When the table is asked for it
lists **every** item, clean ones included:

    | Item | Verdict | Findings |

A table of only the failures cannot be told from one that ran out of budget partway. And it
is still exactly one next step — ranking N items is the writer's job, not the reader's.

## Verdicts and states

**A verdict judges; a state describes.** Most work is graded, and some is better described —
*half done* and *more than one task* are real outcomes no grade carries. Either way the
first word must come from a **declared, fixed set**, never improvised per report, because
that is what lets it grade before the sentence is parsed.

Judging:

`PASS` · `REVISE` · `BLOCKED` · `FAILED` · `IN FLIGHT`

Describing: whatever set the unit declares, defined where it declares them.

Unfinished work still gets a first word; it changes what the line answers, not whether
there is one. **Progress is not a verdict** — "working through the scenarios" is a status,
"six of nine clear, three failing on one cause" is a report.

## When they ask

**Answer the question they asked, and only that one.** Each question has one home:

| They ask | Give | Not |
|---|---|---|
| "what's wrong" / "the findings" | the findings | plus checked, plus trace |
| "why" / "why that way" | the reasoning, attached to what it justifies | a standalone rationale section |
| "what did you check" / "how do you know" | the commands run and what they printed | a restated verdict |
| "is it risky" / "what could bite" | the risks, each with what would resolve it | risks without an ask |
| "where" / "which files" | the trace | a narrative of getting there |
| "show me everything" | all of it, in the order above | — |

**The 30-second cap applies to the detail too.** It is not the place the held-back report
finally lands — a second wall of text costs more than the first, because the reader paid a
question to get it. If the honest answer does not fit, say what it is and offer the rest:
*"12 findings, the 3 that block are below — the other 9 are cosmetic, want them?"*

Severity order, tightest useful shape. A table where the rows are peers:

    | # | Sev | Location | What's wrong | Smallest fix |

**On a PASS, `Checked` is the whole substance** — no findings justify the verdict, so what
was actually run is all that makes it worth anything. Name the command and its result.
Asserting "verified" without the observation is the costliest slop there is; every later
decision rests on it.

**Then stop.** Do not re-offer the remaining sections, do not summarise what was just
given, and do not close with a next step that was already stated. The answer ends when the
question is answered.

## Diagrams

ASCII only, only in the detail, only when the thing has a **shape** — a sequence, a break
in one, a dependency, a before-and-after:

    scrape ──► parse ──► ✗ validate ──► load ──► notify
                          schema drift          (never ran)

One per answer at most. Never in the two-line default. Never for two items, a list that is
already a list, or decoration.

## When this does not fire

A skill that fires on everything turns every reply into a form.

- the answer is one fact and the fact is what was asked
- an acknowledgement — "pushed", "done", "it's at X"
- a discussion, a design proposal, or thinking aloud — a report states a conclusion, it
  does not develop one
- nothing was judged; a status carrying no judgment is a status, and that is fine

## The markers

**The buried verdict.** The judgment lands after the narration, so the reader spends the
attention the report existed to save — twice, if it is bad news.

**The volunteered extra.** Findings, caveats and trace shown unasked, or a "want me to
also…" bolted onto the answer. Both spend the reader on something they did not raise, and
both tax the two lines that mattered.

**Progress dressed as a verdict.** A status with a grade-shaped sentence around it.

**Silent omission.** Asked for findings and given four of seven, with nothing saying so.

**Confidence not matched to method.** A thing fixed on reading and a thing reproduced then
fixed, stated in the same voice. Only the writer knows; say which.

#!/bin/sh
# Find references to things that no longer exist.
#
# Both checks derive what is valid from the tree rather than from a hardcoded
# list, so this script does not go stale when a unit is added, renamed or removed:
#
#   1. every cited `rules/<name>.md` resolves to a file under the plugin
#   2. every cited unit name resolves to a skills/<name>/ directory
#
# Usage:  scripts/check-refs.sh          # scan the repo
#         scripts/check-refs.sh <path>   # scan one file or directory
#
# Exit 0 = clean, 1 = at least one dangling reference.

set -eu

ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
PLUGIN="$ROOT/plugins/agent-workflows"
TARGET="${1:-$ROOT}"
HITS=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$HITS"' EXIT

# --- 1. rules/<name>.md ------------------------------------------------------
grep -rnoI -E 'rules/[a-z-]+\.md' "$TARGET" \
    --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=scripts 2>/dev/null \
| while IFS= read -r hit; do
    rule=${hit##*:}
    loc=${hit%:*}
    # project-profile is check 1b's, so each location is reported once
    [ "$rule" = "rules/project-profile.md" ] && continue
    [ -f "$PLUGIN/$rule" ] && continue
    echo "$loc  ->  $rule (no such file)"
  done >> "$HITS"

# --- 1b. project-profile, however it is spelled ------------------------------
# Caught even without the rules/ prefix: a bare `project-profile.md` mention is
# the same promise to the reader as a full path, and rots the same way.
if [ ! -f "$ROOT/.claude/rules/project-profile.md" ]; then
  grep -rnoI -E 'project-profile(\.md)?' "$TARGET" \
      --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=scripts 2>/dev/null \
  | while IFS= read -r hit; do
      loc=${hit%:*}
      echo "$loc  ->  project-profile (not in this repo)"
    done >> "$HITS"
fi

# --- 2. unit names -----------------------------------------------------------
# Only names shaped like this collection's units are candidates; anything else
# is ordinary hyphenated prose and not ours to resolve.
grep -rnoI -E '[/`](gen|review|reviewing|reporting|ship|setup|doc)-[a-z-]+' "$TARGET" \
    --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=scripts 2>/dev/null \
| while IFS= read -r hit; do
    name=${hit##*:}                 # "/gen-readme" or "`ship-tail"
    name=$(printf '%s' "$name" | tr -d '/`')
    loc=${hit%:*}
    [ -d "$PLUGIN/skills/$name" ] && continue
    echo "$loc  ->  $name (no such skill)"
  done >> "$HITS"

# --- report ------------------------------------------------------------------
sort -u "$HITS" | sed "s|^$ROOT/||"
count=$(sort -u "$HITS" | grep -c . || true)
echo
if [ "$count" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "clean"
  exit 0
fi
echo "$count dangling reference(s)"
exit 1

# CLAUDE.md

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Merge with project-specific instructions as needed.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

---

**These guidelines are working if:** fewer unnecessary changes in diffs, fewer rewrites due to overcomplication, and clarifying questions come before implementation rather than after mistakes.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

---

**These guidelines are working if:** fewer unnecessary changes in diffs, fewer rewrites due to overcomplication, and clarifying questions come before implementation rather than after mistakes.

== plugins/agent-workflows/skills/do-task/SKILL.md ==
---
name: do-task
description: |
  Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
  act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
  why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
  is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
  judges whether it finished.
when_to_use: |
  Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
  it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
  Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
  the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
  claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for
  choosing what to work on, not for opening a change request, and not for deciding whether
  the result is good enough — each of those is somebody else's job.
argument-hint: "[issue-number]"
---

# Do the task

---
name: file-issue
description: |
  Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on, and
  copies the session log beside it wherever one can be had — always attempted, never a
  reason to withhold the issue. Decides first whether the thing needs tracking at all,
  searches for an existing issue before creating a second one, quotes the request in the

---
name: setup-agent-workflows
description: |
  Adopts the agent-workflows plugin into a project — writes the profile sections these
  units resolve against, binds the report contract in CLAUDE.md, and finds the forked
  copies of retired commands that silently shadow the placed ones. Use before the first
  run of ship-create-pr, ship-merge, gen-readme or the reviewing skills, when a unit
  stops because it cannot resolve a project value, or when migrating a repo that holds
  `dw-*` / `qw-*` forks.
---

# Setup agent-workflows

**Placement puts the units where an agent loads them. This is the other half — adoption.**
The placed units describe *some* project; this makes them describe *this* one. It runs once
per repo, and again only to change an answer.

Three things, and the third is the one nobody expects to need:

- **Profile values** — the sections these units resolve against, so no unit stops on an
  unresolvable value
- **The report contract binding** — a line in `CLAUDE.md` that holds every session, rather
  than waiting for a skill to invoke itself
- **Fork migration** — the local copies of retired commands that still appear in the menu
  with nothing announcing which one ran

This is prompt-driven, not a script. Explore, present what you found, confirm, then write.

## It writes only what this plugin owns

A project may place several plugins that all read one `project-profile.md`. The rules are
in `profile-doctrine.md` → "More than one plugin writes this file", and they bind here:
own only what you read, add or update in place and never truncate, and treat a value
already there as a decision rather than something to overwrite.

The sections this plugin owns, and nothing else:
**Labels · Linking & branch · Platform · Git · Docs & diagrams · Reports · Review
semantics.** See [profile-sections.md](./profile-sections.md).

If `agent-workflows-runner` is also placed, its sections — `Paths`, `ID schemes`, the test
front-matter contract, the project's binding and run layer — belong to **its** setup unit.
Leave them alone whether they are present or absent, and say at the end that
`setup-agent-runner` covers them.

## Process

### 1. Explore

Read the repo's actual starting state. Don't assume, and don't ask for anything a command
can answer:

- `git remote get-url origin` — which host, so the CLI and change-request noun are derived
  rather than requested. No remote is a real state; note it and don't guess one
